Red flags: 2026 outcome of the board's investigation into anonymous allegations
- On 15 May 2026 the board announced the completion of an investigation commissioned by a Special Committee of its Audit Committee, begun in December 2025 after anonymous allegations received in October 2025, and carried out by the law firm Barnes & Thornburg and the forensic accounting firm RSM US (museum statement, 15 May 2026).
- The board stated: "The anonymous allegations of fraud, theft, and other malicious conduct were not substantiated", naming among them allegations of sales tax fraud and payroll fraud (museum statement).
- The statement says the investigation "confirmed a long-standing, Board-acknowledged practice" of using art sale proceeds "for purposes beyond strictly the acquisition of art during periods of operating stress", and that the museum plans to repay this internal loan in full by 2030 (museum statement).
- It says "some of the Museum's historical governance, reporting, and recordkeeping practices fell short of the Board's standards" and that the investigation found "certain procedural deficiencies" in the 2025 board officer nominations. It found the director search, "while expedited, was not improperly manipulated" (museum statement).
- The remedial measures listed include mandatory annual governance training for all trustees and a review of the policies on deaccession proceeds and restricted donor funds (museum statement).

SOURCES

Red flags: 2024 to 2025 court challenge over demolishing 142 Free Street
- Greater Portland Landmarks' complaint alleged that city councilors failed to consider Historic Preservation Land Use standards, such as the building's architectural significance, when they voted in May 2024 to declassify 142 Free Street as non-contributing, and asked the Superior Court to vacate the order and send the matter back to the City Council (Maine Public, Carol Bousquet, 20 June 2024).
- The museum argued that alterations over time had diminished the building's historical significance. Director Mark Bessire said: "This appeal questions the judgment of our elected officials and will also impose a significant financial and human resource burden on the City of Portland" (Maine Public, 20 June 2024).
- A Cumberland County Superior Court judge rejected the appeal in late March 2025, siding with the museum (Maine Public, Nicole Ogrysko and Madi Smith, 31 March 2025).
- Kate Lemos McHale, executive director of Greater Portland Landmarks, said she supports the expansion and said: "It doesn't need to come down to a choice between new and old" (Maine Public, 31 March 2025).

SOURCES
- https://www.mainepublic.org/courts-and-crime/2024-06-20/greater-portland-landmarks-files-complaint-against-city-of-portland-over-vote-on-142-free-street
- https://www.mainepublic.org/arts-and-culture/2025-03-31/judge-gives-portland-museum-of-art-the-green-light-to-demolish-the-old-childrens-museum

WIDER CONTEXT
- The Odesa Regional Council dismissed the museum's director, Oleksandr Roitburd, by decision No. 1050-VII of 4 September 2019, citing breaches of several points of his contract (Supreme Court of Ukraine press service, 10 February 2020).
- The Prymorskyi District Court of Odesa ruled on 10 February 2020 that the council's decision was unlawful and cancelled it (Supreme Court of Ukraine press service, 10 February 2020).
- The Odesa Court of Appeal reversed that ruling on 1 June 2020. The stated grounds were holding concerts, refusing council deputies an inspection of the storerooms and carrying out repairs unlawfully; Roitburd objected that the court ruled without the parties present and said the repairs, paid for without state money, saved works from a building in a state of emergency (24 Kanal, 3 June 2020).
- The head of the Odesa Regional State Administration, Maksym Kutsyi, backed Roitburd and said his contract would not be terminated (24 Kanal, 3 June 2020).
- In a ruling of 19 May 2021 the Supreme Court upheld the Prymorskyi court's decision that the dismissal was unlawful and overturned the appeal ruling; the decision is final (Texty.org.ua, 2 June 2021).

- On 12 December 2014 court officials in Tashkent said three former senior employees of the Tashkent State Arts Museum had been sentenced to prison for fraud: the former senior curator Mirfaizi Usmanov to nine years and three months, and the former head of the restoration lab and a restorer to eight years each (Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, 12 December 2014).
- They were found guilty of replacing paintings by Soviet artists with copies between 1999 and 2014 and selling the originals to unknown individuals; authorities said they did the same with about 25 paintings from the museum's European art collection.
